gaps.robot_results: No published count of pythons detected or removed at robot-rabbit pens.
gaps.fleet_size: Coverage differs (40 rebuilt toy rabbits per ABC; 120 deployed per AP; about 90 per a 2026 secondary report). Use only what a fetched source states.
gaps.causation: The robots replaced live rabbit lures because live rabbits were costly to keep; do not say the robots exist because pythons ate the wild rabbits.

sources.title: Python Action Team - Removing Invasive Constrictors (PATRIC)
sources.publisher: Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission

facts.fact: After this program launched in spring 2017, the number and rate of Burmese pythons removed from the wild increased.
As of April 2025, over 23,500 pythons have been removed from natural areas in the state of Florida; over 11,000 by FWC PATRIC and SFWMD PEP contractors since program inception.
Researchers released 95 adult marsh rabbits in areas of the Everglades known to harbor pythons; within 11 months pythons accounted for 77 percent of rabbit deaths.
SFWMD Python Elimination Program grows bigger with Broward and Collier counties expansion (June 16, 2017).

sources.title: DYK: Using Robotic Rabbits to Remove Invasive Pythons

facts.fact: Scientists from the District and the University of Florida have teamed up to use robotic rabbit decoys.
Solar-powered, remote-controlled robots designed to look like rabbits produce a heat signature and emit a smell designed to attract pythons.
The robots are equipped with cameras that monitor for pythons and notify District officials when a snake is detected, so a python removal agent can be dispatched.

sources.title: Mammalian lures monitored with time-lapse cameras increase detection of pythons and other snakes (PeerJ 12:e17577)

facts.fact: We recorded 21 independent detections of pythons at treatment pens with lures and one detection at a control pen without lures.
Time-lapse cameras detected almost 40 times more snakes than visual surveys; we did not detect any pythons with python detection dogs.
Domesticated rabbits were used as live lures in pens monitored with time-lapse game cameras.

sources.title: Marsh rabbit mortalities tie pythons to the precipitous decline of mammals in the Everglades
sources.publisher: U.S. Geological Survey (Proceedings of the Royal Society B)

facts.fact: Pythons accounted for 77% of rabbit mortalities within 11 months of their translocation to Everglades National Park, and python predation appeared to preclude the persistence of rabbit populations in the park.
On control sites outside the park, no rabbits were killed by pythons.

sources.title: Estimating detection probability for Burmese Pythons with few detections and zero recapture events

facts.fact: Detection probability ranged from 0.0001 to 0.0146; detection probabilities for Burmese Pythons are therefore likely below 0.05.
Traditional capture-recapture or visual surveys are unlikely to yield accurate information on python population size or trends without cost-prohibitive effort.

sources.title: Mammalian scent lures fail to increase detections of invasive Burmese pythons

facts.fact: Mammalian scent lures alone are insufficient to attract pythons; since live mammals can attract pythons but scent lures cannot, future studies could examine a lure combining heat, visual and movement stimuli.

sources.title: Florida snake hunters deploy robotic rabbits to capture invasive Burmese pythons

facts.fact: The researchers replaced the stuffing in 40 toy rabbits with electrical components powered by solar energy and waterproofed them.
Robert McCleery, a University of Florida wildlife ecologist: 'We want to capture all of the processes that an actual rabbit would give off.'

sources.title: Florida enlists robot bunnies to manage invasive pythons

facts.fact: Officials hope to have preliminary results by next summer.

Burmese pythons are not native to Florida; they were brought through the exotic pet trade and escaped their enclosures or were released, said Mike Kirkland of the South Florida Water Management District.
The pythons have reduced the population of fur-bearing animals by up to 95%, he explained.
